atl0: Jumper’s Knee (Patellar Tendinopathy): Exercises and Treatment | İhsan Eren
atl1: Pain just below the kneecap that gets worse when jumping and going downstairs: what causes jumper’s knee, and how is a progressive loading programme done? Symptoms, advice and six exercises to do at home.
atl3: Jumper’s knee is pain in the tendon just below the kneecap (the patellar tendon) caused by overloading it. It is common in sports that involve jumping, such as volleyball and basketball, but it can also affect people who do not play sport. Rest alone is often not enough; the core of treatment is exercise that gets the tendon used to load again, step by step.

atl14: The diagnosis is usually made from your symptoms and an examination; a scan is often not needed.
atl15: Too much load on the tendon: lots of walking, running downhill.
atl17: Weakness in the front thigh muscle, sometimes with weak hip muscles too.
atl18: It is most common between the teenage years and the thirties, but it can happen at any age.
atl20: In a study of 76 patients in the Netherlands, most participants had had pain for about two years. Half were assigned to a four-stage programme and half to slow-lowering (eccentric) squats on a slope only. After 24 weeks the progressive programme group had improved more; 43% versus 27% returned to sport, but this difference was not statistically significant.
atl21: The four stages of the programme
atl22: Tensing the muscle without moving: such as a wall sit, 45 seconds, 5 times.
atl23: Slow strength exercises: lunges, step-ups or a leg press machine.
atl26: Participants moved on to the next stage when pain during a single-leg squat was 3 out of 10 or less and the current stage had been done for at least a week.
atl28: You can cut down on activities that make the pain worse, such as running, jumping, and long or hilly walks. The tendon needs load to heal, but too much makes the pain worse.
atl30: You can make sure pain during exercise does not go above 3 out of 10. When an exercise becomes pain-free, move on to the next one.
atl32: You can apply ice wrapped in a towel for 10–15 minutes, 2–3 times a day.
atl34: A jumper’s knee strap worn just below the kneecap can reduce the load on the tendon. You can ask your pharmacist which painkiller is suitable.
atl35: For pain around the kneecap, see the anterior knee pain guide; for tendon pain above the heel, see the Achilles tendinopathy guide.
atl36: Six exercises to strengthen the tendon
atl37: Work through them in order: do not move on to the next exercise until the current one is pain-free. Pain during exercise should not go above 3 out of 10.
atl39: Lean your back against a wall and slide down until your knees are at roughly a right angle; if this is hard, stay higher up. Hold still. Pain should not go above 3 out of 10. As it gets easier, you can put more of your weight on the painful leg.
atl42: Start once the half squat against the wall is pain-free. Holding lightly onto a worktop, stand on your painful leg and bend your knee as far as is comfortable; do not let your knee drop inwards. Then push back up.
atl43: Will it get better if I rest?
atl44: The tendon needs load to heal, but too much load makes the pain worse. Rather than resting completely, you can cut down on running, jumping and long walks that make the pain worse and start gradual exercise.
atl46: It can often take months. In a study of athletes, most of whom had had symptoms for about two years, fewer than half had returned to their previous level of sport by 24 weeks. Regular, patient exercise matters.
atl48: You can carry on as far as the pain allows, with a reduced load. In the study, athletes moved on to the next stage and gradually returned to sport once pain during a single-leg squat was 3 out of 10 or less. When symptoms flared up, they were advised to stop or substantially reduce activity for at least 4 weeks.
atl49: How is it different from anterior knee pain?
atl50: In jumper’s knee the pain is just below the kneecap, over the tendon. In anterior knee pain the pain is felt more around and behind the kneecap. For details, see our anterior knee pain guide.
